subject: physics
topicDisplay: Theme A.3 Work, energy and power
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Work done as a transfer of energy
Read and draw a Sankey diagram
Work by a constant force at an angle to the displacement
Work by the resultant force equals the change in kinetic energy
Mechanical energy is conserved when no resistive forces act
Calculate kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy
Power as the rate of doing work
Calculate efficiency from energy or power

questions.q: Work done and energy are both measured in joules. Which statement correctly defines one joule of work done?
options: The work done when a force of 1 N acts on a body for a time of 1 s, whether or not the body moves at all.
The work done when a force of 1 N moves its point of application 1 m in the direction of the force.
The work done when a force of 1 N acts on a body that moves 1 m in any direction relative to that force.
The energy that a force of 1 N contains, whatever body it acts on or however it moves.
optionWhy: A student who thinks work depends on how long a force acts picks this. A force of 1 N for 1 s gives an impulse of 1 N s, which is a change of momentum, not a measure of the energy transferred. If the body does not move, no work is done at all.
W = Fs cos θ = 1 N × 1 m × cos 0° = 1 N m = 1 J. Work and energy share the joule because the work done by a force IS the energy it transfers.

A student who ignores the direction of the force picks this. If the body moves 1 m perpendicular to the 1 N force, the force does no work; only the component along the displacement counts (W = Fs cos θ).

A student who treats force and energy as the same thing picks this. A force does not contain energy; it transfers energy only when its point of application moves, and 1 J is transferred by 1 N acting through 1 m.
questions.explain: W = Fs cos θ = 1 N × 1 m × cos 0° = 1 N m = 1 J. Work and energy share the joule because the work done by a force IS the energy it transfers.
questions.working: W = Fs cos θ = (1 N)(1 m)(cos 0°) = 1 N m = 1 J.

questions.q: A student draws a Sankey diagram for an electric motor. The input arrow is 50 mm wide and represents 100 J of electrical energy. Only two output arrows are drawn: one 20 mm wide for work done lifting a load, and one 25 mm wide for thermal energy transferred to the surroundings. Which statement about the diagram is correct?
options: An arrow is missing, but it only represents 5 J, as 1 mm of width stands for 1 J.
No arrow is missing; the other 10 J was used up inside the motor and is gone.
The lifting arrow should be widest, as it shows the motor's useful output.
An arrow 5 mm wide is missing; it represents 10 J, since the outputs must total 100 J.
optionWhy: A student who reads widths straight off as joules picks this. The scale here is 100 J ÷ 50 mm = 2 J per mm, so the missing 5 mm width represents 10 J, not 5 J.

A student who thinks energy is used up picks this. The motor cannot destroy energy; the 10 J went somewhere, such as sound or further heating, and a correct Sankey diagram must show it so that the outputs equal the input.

A student who assumes a device's useful output must dominate picks this. The width is set by the actual energy transferred. A motor that lifts 40 J of every 100 J supplied is realistic, and its useful arrow need not be the widest.

The scale is 100 J ÷ 50 mm = 2 J per mm. The two arrows total 45 mm, which is 90 J, so 10 J (5 mm) is unaccounted for. By conservation of energy the output widths must add up to the input width, so an arrow for this energy, for example sound, is missing.
questions.explain: The scale is 100 J ÷ 50 mm = 2 J per mm. The two arrows total 45 mm, which is 90 J, so 10 J (5 mm) is unaccounted for. By conservation of energy the output widths must add up to the input width, so an arrow for this energy, for example sound, is missing.
questions.working: Scale = 100 J / 50 mm = 2 J mm⁻¹. Outputs drawn = 20 mm + 25 mm = 45 mm = 90 J. Missing = 50 mm − 45 mm = 5 mm = 5 mm × 2 J mm⁻¹ = 10 J.

questions.q: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.60 m at constant speed on a smooth, horizontal table. The tension in the string is 12 N. How much work does the tension do on the stone during one complete revolution?
options: About 45 J, which is the tension multiplied by the full circumference of the circular path.
Zero, because the tension is perpendicular to the stone's displacement at every instant.
A positive amount, because the tension is the force that keeps the stone moving.
Zero, because the tension is balanced by an equal outward centrifugal force on the stone.
optionWhy: A student who multiplies force by distance travelled whatever the direction picks this (12 N × 2π × 0.60 m ≈ 45 J). The tension has no component along the stone's direction of motion, so it does no work.

The tension points to the centre of the circle, while the stone's displacement at each instant is along the tangent, so θ = 90° and W = Fs cos 90° = 0 throughout. This is why the stone's speed, and so its kinetic energy, stays constant.

A student who thinks a force is needed to keep a body moving picks this. The stone would keep moving without the tension, in a straight line; the tension only changes its direction, and a force perpendicular to the motion transfers no energy.

A student who believes a real outward centrifugal force balances the tension picks this: no resultant force, so no work. The reasoning is wrong. In an inertial frame there is no outward force; the resultant force on the stone is the inward tension. It does no work only because it is perpendicular to the stone's displacement at every instant, so W = Fs cos 90° = 0.
questions.explain: The tension points to the centre of the circle, while the stone's displacement at each instant is along the tangent, so θ = 90° and W = Fs cos 90° = 0 throughout. This is why the stone's speed, and so its kinetic energy, stays constant.

questions.q: A trolley moves 4.0 m in a straight line. One of the forces acting on it is a constant 20 N force directed at 120° to the trolley's displacement. How much work does this force do on the trolley?
optionWhy: A student who believes work cannot be negative drops the sign. cos 120° = −0.50, so the work done is −40 J: the force takes 40 J of energy from the trolley.
A student who multiplies force by distance without the angle gets 20 × 4.0 = 80 J. Only the component along the displacement does work, and here that component points backwards.
A student who uses sin 120° = 0.866 gets 20 × 4.0 × 0.866 = 69 J. The work uses the cosine of the angle between the force and the displacement, and cos 120° is negative.
W = Fs cos θ = 20 × 4.0 × cos 120° = 80 × (−0.50) = −40 J. The force has a component opposite to the displacement, so it transfers energy away from the trolley.
questions.explain: W = Fs cos θ = 20 × 4.0 × cos 120° = 80 × (−0.50) = −40 J. The force has a component opposite to the displacement, so it transfers energy away from the trolley.

questions.q: A student pulls a crate at constant velocity for 5.0 m across a rough, level floor, using a horizontal force of 60 N. Which statement about the work done on the crate is correct?
options: The pull does 300 J of work on the crate, so the crate's kinetic energy increases by 300 J.
The pull must be greater than friction, so the resultant force does positive work on it.
The resultant force does no work, so the crate's kinetic energy does not change.
Friction does no work, because a force opposing the motion cannot do work.
optionWhy: A student who equates the work done by one force with the change in kinetic energy picks this. The pull does 300 J of work, but friction does −300 J; the change in kinetic energy equals the work done by the resultant force, which is zero.

A student who thinks motion needs a resultant force picks this. The crate moves at constant velocity, so by Newton's first law the resultant force is zero; if the pull exceeded friction the crate would speed up.

At constant velocity the resultant force is zero: the 60 N pull is balanced by 60 N of friction. The pull does +300 J of work and friction does −300 J, so the work done by the resultant force is zero and the kinetic energy is unchanged. The 300 J ends up as internal energy of the crate and floor.

A student who believes work cannot be negative picks this. Friction acts at 180° to the displacement, so it does W = 60 × 5.0 × cos 180° = −300 J of work, transferring energy from the crate to internal energy.
questions.explain: At constant velocity the resultant force is zero: the 60 N pull is balanced by 60 N of friction. The pull does +300 J of work and friction does −300 J, so the work done by the resultant force is zero and the kinetic energy is unchanged. The 300 J ends up as internal energy of the crate and floor.

questions.q: A block of mass 0.40 kg hangs from a vertical spring of spring constant 50 N m⁻¹. At one instant the block is moving at 1.5 m s⁻¹, its centre is 0.30 m above the level chosen as the zero of gravitational potential energy, and the spring is stretched by 0.20 m from its natural length. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the mechanical energy of the block–spring–Earth system at this instant?
optionWhy: Mechanical energy is the sum of all three stores: E_k = ½ × 0.40 × 1.5² = 0.45 J, E_p = 0.40 × 9.8 × 0.30 = 1.18 J and E_H = ½ × 50 × 0.20² = 1.0 J, giving 2.6 J. The internal energy of the block and spring is not part of mechanical energy.

A student who takes mechanical energy to be kinetic plus gravitational potential energy only gets 0.45 + 1.18 = 1.6 J. The stretched spring stores elastic potential energy, ½k(Δx)² = 1.0 J, and this is part of the system's mechanical energy.
A student who uses E_k = mv² instead of ½mv² gets 0.90 J for the kinetic energy and a total of 3.1 J. Kinetic energy is ½mv², so the block's kinetic energy is 0.45 J and the total is 2.6 J.
A student who writes the elastic potential energy as ½kΔx, dropping the square, gets ½ × 50 × 0.20 = 5.0 J for the spring and a total of 6.6 J. The extension must be squared: E_H = ½k(Δx)² = 1.0 J.
questions.explain: Mechanical energy is the sum of all three stores: E_k = ½ × 0.40 × 1.5² = 0.45 J, E_p = 0.40 × 9.8 × 0.30 = 1.18 J and E_H = ½ × 50 × 0.20² = 1.0 J, giving 2.6 J. The internal energy of the block and spring is not part of mechanical energy.
questions.working:
Mechanical energy = E_k + E_p + E_H.
E_k = ½mv² = ½ × 0.40 kg × (1.5 m s⁻¹)² = 0.45 J.
E_p = mgh = 0.40 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × 0.30 m = 1.176 J.
E_H = ½k(Δx)² = ½ × 50 N m⁻¹ × (0.20 m)² = 1.0 J.
Total = 0.45 + 1.176 + 1.0 = 2.626 J ≈ 2.6 J (2 s.f.).

questions.q: Blocks of mass 2.0 kg and 4.0 kg are released from rest at the same height. The 2.0 kg block slides down a steep ramp and the 4.0 kg block down a shallow ramp; the bottoms of the two ramps are at the same level. Both ramps are frictionless and air resistance is negligible. How do their speeds at the bottom compare?
options: The 4.0 kg block is faster, because its weight is twice as large.
The lighter block is faster, because its steeper ramp gives it more acceleration.
The 4.0 kg block is faster, because it accelerates for longer on its ramp.
They are equal, as each block loses the same potential energy per kilogram.
optionWhy: A student who thinks heavier objects fall faster picks this. The 4.0 kg block has twice the weight but also twice the mass to accelerate; its kinetic energy per kilogram, gΔh, is the same as the lighter block's.

A student who equates larger acceleration with larger final speed picks this. The steep ramp does give more acceleration, but over a shorter distance; the speed at the bottom depends only on the height dropped.

A student who thinks a longer time accelerating means a greater speed picks this. On the shallow ramp the acceleration is smaller, which exactly offsets the longer time; the final speed is √(2gΔh) on both ramps.
With no frictional or resistive forces, mechanical energy is conserved: mgΔh = ½mv², so v = √(2gΔh). Mass cancels and the path shape does not appear, so both blocks reach the same speed.
questions.explain: With no frictional or resistive forces, mechanical energy is conserved: mgΔh = ½mv², so v = √(2gΔh). Mass cancels and the path shape does not appear, so both blocks reach the same speed.

questions.q: A spring of spring constant 180 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 0.10 m and then released to launch a trolley of mass 0.50 kg along a smooth horizontal track. All the elastic potential energy is transferred to the trolley's kinetic energy. What is the speed of the trolley?
options: 6.0 m s⁻¹
2.7 m s⁻¹
1.9 m s⁻¹
1.3 m s⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who treats elastic energy as proportional to the compression writes ½ × 180 × 0.10 = 9.0 J and gets v = √(2 × 9.0 / 0.50) = 6.0 m s⁻¹. E_H = ½k(Δx)², so Δx must be squared.

A student who multiplies the final force by the compression writes 18 N × 0.10 m = 1.8 J and gets v = √(2 × 1.8 / 0.50) = 2.7 m s⁻¹. The spring force rises from zero to 18 N, so the energy stored is half of this: 0.90 J.
A student who uses E_k = mv² without the ½ gets v = √(0.90 / 0.50) = 1.3 m s⁻¹. With ½mv² = 0.90 J, v² = 3.6 m² s⁻².

questions.q: An electric hoist raises a load of weight 1600 N vertically at a constant speed of 0.45 m s⁻¹. What is the power developed by the hoist's upward force on the load?
optionWhy: At constant speed the upward force equals the weight, 1600 N. P = Fv = 1600 × 0.45 = 720 W = 7.2 × 10² W.
A student who divides force by speed gets 1600 / 0.45 = 3556 W. Power is force multiplied by speed, P = Fv, because P = FΔs/Δt.
A student who treats the 1600 N weight as a mass and multiplies by g gets 1600 × 9.8 × 0.45 = 7056 W. The load's weight is already a force in newtons.
A student who equates power with force gives 1600 W, the size of the force. Power also depends on how fast the force moves its point of application: P = Fv.
questions.explain: At constant speed the upward force equals the weight, 1600 N. P = Fv = 1600 × 0.45 = 720 W = 7.2 × 10² W.
questions.working: At constant speed, F = weight = 1600 N. P = Fv = (1600 N)(0.45 m s⁻¹) = 720 W = 7.2 × 10² W.

questions.q: An electric motor with an efficiency of 0.60 takes an input power of 1.5 kW. It lifts a load of mass 90 kg vertically at constant speed. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the speed of the load?
optionWhy: Useful power out = η × total power in = 0.60 × 1500 = 900 W. At constant speed P = Fv with F = mg = 90 × 9.8 = 882 N, so v = 900 / 882 = 1.02 m s⁻¹.
A student who assumes all the input power is useful gets v = 1500 / 882 = 1.70 m s⁻¹. Energy is conserved in total, but 40% of the input is dissipated, so only 900 W lifts the load.
A student who divides by the efficiency uses 1500 / 0.60 = 2500 W and gets v = 2500 / 882 = 2.83 m s⁻¹. The useful output must be smaller than the input: useful power = 0.60 × 1500 W.
A student who uses the mass, 90 kg, in place of the weight gets v = 900 / 90 = 10.0 m s⁻¹. The force needed is the weight, mg = 882 N.
questions.explain: Useful power out = η × total power in = 0.60 × 1500 = 900 W. At constant speed P = Fv with F = mg = 90 × 9.8 = 882 N, so v = 900 / 882 = 1.02 m s⁻¹.
questions.working: Useful power out = ηP_in = 0.60 × 1500 W = 900 W. F = mg = (90 kg)(9.8 m s⁻²) = 882 N. v = P/F = 900 W / 882 N = 1.02 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: Hydrogen gas at atmospheric pressure releases 120 MJ of energy per kilogram and 0.011 MJ per litre when burned. Petrol releases 46 MJ per kilogram and 34 MJ per litre. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
options: A litre of hydrogen releases about 2.6 times the energy of a litre of petrol.
A litre of petrol releases about 3000 times as much energy as a litre of hydrogen.
A kilogram of petrol releases more energy than a kilogram of hydrogen, as petrol is denser.
Hydrogen releases its energy about 2.6 times faster than petrol does when it is burned.
optionWhy: A student who assumes energy per kilogram and energy per litre rank fuels the same way applies the per-kilogram ratio (120 / 46 ≈ 2.6) to volume. The per-litre data show the opposite: petrol releases about 3000 times more per litre.

Per litre: 34 MJ ÷ 0.011 MJ ≈ 3.1 × 10³, so about 3000 times as much. Although hydrogen releases about 2.6 times more energy per kilogram, its density as a gas is so low that a litre contains very little mass. This is why hydrogen vehicles must store it highly compressed or liquefied.

A student who thinks denser fuels contain more energy per kilogram picks this. The data show hydrogen releases 120 MJ per kilogram against petrol's 46 MJ; density affects energy per litre, not per kilogram.

A student who confuses the amount of energy with the rate of transfer picks this. Energy released per kilogram says how MUCH energy a fuel gives, not how quickly; the rate depends on how fast the fuel is burned.
questions.explain: Per litre: 34 MJ ÷ 0.011 MJ ≈ 3.1 × 10³, so about 3000 times as much. Although hydrogen releases about 2.6 times more energy per kilogram, its density as a gas is so low that a litre contains very little mass. This is why hydrogen vehicles must store it highly compressed or liquefied.
questions.working: Per litre: 34 MJ / 0.011 MJ = 3.1 × 10³ ≈ 3000. Per kilogram: 120 MJ / 46 MJ = 2.6 (hydrogen higher).
